title: Built environment color modulates autonomic and EEG indices of emotional response
research_question: To investigate if the blue ambient wall color of an interior room would result in modulation of autonomic, EEG, and self-report indicators of emotion, and if participant changes in self-reported emotion correspond with measures of autonomic and central nervous system modulations.

participants.description: Eighteen right-handed adult participants (8 women, mean age = 34.5±9.87 years) with normal or corrected-to-normal vision, able to speak and read English, no prior psychiatric, neurological, or neurodevelopmental conditions, and no prior experience or training in built environment design.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Cave Automatic Virtual Environment (CAVE) displaying three conditions: 1) Resting state (black, no built environment), 2) Control (white room, R255, G255, B255, hue=0, saturation=0, brightness=100), 3) Condition (blue room, Dulux 'Post Boy A359' R122, G155, B173, hue=198, saturation=35.3, brightness=67.8). Each scene lasted two minutes, with a black resting state displayed between conditions for self-report assessment. The virtual room included a closed door and a chair.

mechanisms: The visually salient nature of the color condition resulted in increased autonomic response.
Modulations of brain activity (EEG frontal hemispheric lateralization and midline power in alpha bandwidth, and power spectral density in theta, alpha, beta) are linked to emotional processing.
Higher frontal left hemispheric lateralization is associated with positive emotions.

The lack of correspondence between self-report and physiological/neural measures may indicate that emotions are not accurately identified/expressed or that responses occur without conscious processing.
moderators: Time of day (analyzed a-posteriori and confirmed not to influence responsivity to color)
implementation_implications: Built environment design, specifically color, has the potential to modulate emotional response, delivering public health, economic, and social benefits.
Changing the color of space (e.g., through paint) is an economic and practical design characteristic to alter in existing buildings, requiring no structural changes.
Color changes increase accessibility for a broader portion of the population to modify their environment, especially in rental markets or shared residences.

limitations: The blue color condition was presented at the end of the experiment (after scale conditions), preventing randomization of order and potentially violating expectation.
The study could not disentangle the effects of hue, saturation, and brightness as the blue stimulus differed from the white stimulus in colorimetric dimensions.
The room was not symmetrical in furnishings, which could influence brain activity regions.
The sample consisted of healthy adults with normal or corrected-to-normal vision and no prior psychiatric/neurological conditions, limiting generalizability.
The study did not include an assessment of participants' color vision perception.
The true colors from a spectrometer were not reported, only the rendered values.

paper_metadata.title: Built environment color modulates autonomic and EEG indices of emotional response
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Built environment color modulates autonomic and <scp>EEG</scp> indices of emotional response
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: AbstractUnderstanding built environment exposure as a component of environmental enrichment has significant implications for mental health, but little is known about the effects design characteristics have on our emotions and associated neurophysiology. Using a Cave Automatic Virtual Environment while monitoring indoor environmental quality (IEQ), 18 participants were exposed to a resting state (black), and two room scenes, control (white) and condition (blue), to understand if the color of the virtual walls affected self‐report, autonomic nervous system, and central nervous system correlates of emotion. Our findings showed that exposure to the chromatic color condition (blue) compared to the achromatic control (white) and resting‐state (black, no built environment) significantly increased the range in respiration and skin conductance response. We also detected a significant increase in alpha frontal midline power and frontal hemispheric lateralization relative to blue condition, and increased power spectral density across all electrodes in the blue condition for theta, alpha, and beta bandwidths. The ability for built environment design to modulate emotional response has the potential to deliver significant public health, economic, and social benefits to the entire community. The findings show that blue coloring of the built environment increases autonomic range and is associated with modulations of brain activity linked to emotional processing.
